name: Crime in India (annual report series, 1953-2024)
publisher: National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Ministry of Home Affairs
lag: 12-24 months; 12 mo for CII-2022, ~21 mo for CII-2023, ~16 mo for CII-2024
taxonomy: IPC+SLL up to 2023; IPC(Jan-Jun)+BNS(Jul-Dec) for 2024; BNS+SLL from 2025
license: unstated (GoI publication; GODL-India applies to the data.gov.in mirror)
caveats: principal-offence-rule: only the most serious offence per FIR is counted, so rape/robbery inside a murder FIR vanish from the counts
reported crime (FIR registrations), not victimisation or conviction; refusal-to-register and non-cognisable offences are invisible

IPC->BNS break at 2024-07-01 splits the 2024 reference year across two statute books; 'simple hurt' became non-cognisable and Hurt cases fell 30.58% (6.36 lakh -> 4.41 lakh) for definitional reasons alone
district lists change every year with state reorganisation; no stable district key is published
crime rates use projected population from the 2011 Census; no Census since 2011
district-wise tables were NOT released for reference years 2016 and 2017
main numbered chapters are State/UT-level and Metropolitan-City-level; district data ships as separate supplementary tables
evidence: Could not open ncrb.gov.in: blocked by this environment's egress proxy for both WebFetch and curl (CONNECT tunnel 403). Search engine returned indexed NCRB PDF URLs with matching titles for CII 2019 Vol 3, CII 2022 Book 1, CII 2023 Part I and CII 2024 Volume II. Wikipedia 'Crime in India' confirms the 2023 edition cites Vol 1, Vol 2 and Vol 3.
how_to_obtain: Download PDFs from ncrb.gov.in from an Indian IP or any unblocked network. The publication index is at ncrb.gov.in/en/crime-india; the table/chapter contents index is at ncrb.gov.in/crime-in-india-table-addtional-table-and-chapter-contents.
notes: The backbone series and the benchmark every other source is validated against. Three volumes since the 2017 format revamp. Chapter letter suffix encodes geography: 'A' chapters = States/UTs, 'B'/'D' chapters = Metropolitan Cities (e.g. 3A Crime Against Women States/UTs, 3B Crime Against Women Metropolitan Cities, 4A Crime Against Children).

name: Crime in India 2024 (latest published edition)
lag: ~16 months (reference year ends Dec 2024, released 6 May 2026)
caveats: First edition to carry BNS/BNSS/BSA crime heads; NOT comparable with 2023 or earlier at crime-head level
Headline 6% national decline (58.85 lakh cases in 2024 vs 62.41 lakh in 2023) is substantially a definitional artefact of the BNS switch, per NCRB's own attribution
2024 is a split year: IPC applies 1 Jan - 30 Jun 2024, BNS from 1 Jul 2024
principal-offence-rule applies
evidence: Search engine indexed https://www.ncrb.gov.in/uploads/files/2CrimeinIndia2024-VolumeII.pdf (title 'Ncrb'), confirming the Volume II file naming for the 2024 edition. Multiple secondary sources (Vision IAS dated 2026-05-07, The Wire) put the release at 6 May 2026 and report 58.85 lakh cases, -6% YoY, cybercrime +17%, crime against women -1.5%, children +5.9%, senior citizens +16.9%.
how_to_obtain: Direct PDF download; substitute '1'/'3' for '2' in the filename prefix to reach the other volumes (pattern unverified).
notes: AS OF 2026-09-19 THIS IS THE MOST RECENT CRIME IN INDIA EDITION PUBLISHED. Crime in India 2025 is not out; on past form expect it somewhere between mid-2026 and mid-2027.

name: Crime in India 2023
caveats: Last fully-IPC edition; the clean end-point of the 1953-2023 IPC series
principal-offence-rule applies
Crime rate 448.3 per lakh population (up from 422.2 in 2022); denominator is a projection off the 2011 Census
evidence: Search engine indexed https://www.ncrb.gov.in/uploads/files/1CrimeinIndia2023PartI.pdf under the title 'NCRB Crime in India Report 2023'. Secondary sources report release 29-30 Sept 2025, 62.41 lakh total cognisable cases (+7.2%), rate 448.3/lakh.
how_to_obtain: Direct PDF download from ncrb.gov.in (blocked from this environment).
notes: Use 2023 as the last IPC-comparable base year for any time-series map. Note the 2023 file naming switched to /uploads/files/ and 'PartI' rather than the older /uploads/nationalcrimerecordsbureau/custom/<epoch>_ pattern.

name: Crime in India 2022 (Book 1 / Volume I)
caveats: principal-offence-rule applies
4,45,256 crimes against women recorded in 2022 (Ch.3, Table 3A.1)
evidence: URL indexed with title 'National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) 2022 report'. The embedded unix timestamp 1701607577 decodes to 2023-12-03 12:46 UTC, dating the upload and hence the release to early December 2023 (~12-month lag). A secondary academic source cites 'NCRB 2022, Chapter 3, Table 3A.1, p.211' as the crimes-against-women State/UT table.
how_to_obtain: Direct PDF download; also mirrored at ruralindiaonline.org (Volumes I and II) and at endnowfoundation.org for 2021.
notes: The /custom/<epoch>_ filename pattern lets you date any NCRB upload precisely. Useful for reconstructing the publication-lag series without press coverage.

name: Crime in India - Additional Tables and Chapter Contents (district-wise supplementary tables)
caveats: District-wise data is NOT in the numbered chapters of Volumes 1-3; those are State/UT and Metropolitan-City level. It is published as a separate 'Additional Tables' set
No district-wise release at all for reference years 2016 and 2017, and no machine-readable release for those two years
District keys are police districts, not revenue districts (strong prior, unverified in this session)
evidence: Search engine returned the URL https://ncrb.gov.in/crime-in-india-table-addtional-table-and-chapter-contents (note NCRB's own typo 'addtional') in response to a query for the exact NCRB table title 'Crime Head-wise & District-wise Cases Registered'. Page could not be opened: ncrb.gov.in is egress-blocked here.
how_to_obtain: Open the page from an unblocked network and enumerate every linked table file per year. THIS IS THE SINGLE HIGHEST-VALUE VERIFICATION STEP IN THIS DOSSIER.
notes: Exact district table numbers could NOT be confirmed. What is confirmed: chapter numbering uses a letter suffix for geography (1A Summary States/UTs, 2A/2B Murder, 2C/2D Kidnapping & Abduction, 3A Crime Against Women States/UTs, 3B Crime Against Women Metropolitan Cities, 4A Crime Against Children, 5 Juveniles in Conflict with Law). District tables sit outside that scheme.

name: Crime in India - Metropolitan Cities chapters (3B, 2B, 2D etc.) and Mega Cities tables
geo_coverage: 19 metropolitan cities in the main chapters; 34 and 53 cities in supplementary tables
time_start: unknown (city chapter present at least since 2014 format)
caveats: City units are police-commissionerate jurisdictions, not municipal boundaries; they do not nest cleanly inside revenue districts

Denominators are urban-agglomeration populations larger than municipal limits; for Delhi, NCRB uses the whole National Capital Region (incl. Faridabad, Ghaziabad, Gurgaon, Noida), which deflates Delhi's crime rate
Only 19 cities in the main chapters against 77 police commissionerates nationally - most commissionerate cities have no separate NCRB row
Double counting risk: a city's cases may also be inside its parent state total, and possibly inside a district row
evidence: ORF analysis 'Crime in India's largest cities' states the metropolitan chapter reports 19 urban agglomerations, additional tables cover 34 metropolitan cities, and a 'Miscellaneous Mega Cities' set covers 53; it also states there are 77 police commissionerates nationally and that NCRB uses NCR population for Delhi. Wikipedia 'Crime in India' shows violent-crime tables across 19 major cities for 2020 and 2021.
how_to_obtain: Same PDFs as the parent report.
notes: THIS IS THE CENTRAL MAPPING HAZARD. For any city with a commissionerate, the city row and the surrounding district row are different polygons and may overlap or double count. Resolve per state before rendering.

name: Crime in India historical editions (1953 to ~2013)
taxonomy: IPC+SLL (old crime-head list, several definition changes)
caveats: Older editions are scanned image PDFs requiring OCR; table layouts change repeatedly
Crime-head definitions changed several times (e.g. rape definition widened after the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013), breaking the series at 2013
Pre-2014 volume/table structure differs from the post-2017 three-volume format
evidence: NCRB is documented as publishing crime data since 1953 and Wikipedia's 'Crime in India' cites statistics from 1953 onward; the specific archive page listing pre-2014 PDFs could not be opened.
how_to_obtain: Browse the Crime in India publication index on ncrb.gov.in; for years missing there, use the Dataful/Factly compilations which claim coverage back to the 1950s-60s for headline series.
notes: Only worth OCRing if the product needs long-run trend lines. For a police.uk-style map, 2014 onward is enough.

name: Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India (ADSI)
taxonomy: custom (accidental-death and suicide cause taxonomy, not IPC/BNS)
caveats: Suicide and road-death counts are police-recorded, and are known to be materially lower than Million Death Study / civil registration estimates
The city tables cover the same ~53 metropolitan cities as Crime in India; true district-level coverage is thinner than the report's framing suggests and must be checked table by table
Cause-of-suicide categories are police judgement calls, not clinical determinations
Road accident data here overlaps and disagrees with MoRTH 'Road Accidents in India'
evidence: Search engine returned the NCRB ADSI landing page (title 'Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India (ADSI) Reports') and the file https://www.ncrb.gov.in/uploads/files/1ADSIPublication-2023.pdf. Secondary reporting confirms ADSI 2024 released alongside Crime in India 2024 in May 2026 with 1,70,746 suicides recorded in 2024. OpenCity hosts an 'Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India 2024' dataset with the full report.
how_to_obtain: Direct PDF download from ncrb.gov.in; the OpenCity CKAN mirror at data.opencity.in/dataset/accidental-deaths-and-suicides-in-india-2024 carries the same file.
notes: Relevant to a safety map for road-traffic death density, not for crime per se. Treat as a separate layer with its own caveat text.

name: Prison Statistics India (PSI)
caveats: Jail-level tables exist (jail name, type, capacity, inmates) but crime attribution is by the committing state, not by where the offence happened - useless for locating crime
Undertrials are 73% of the population, so offence mix reflects arrest patterns, not convictions
Occupancy is a point-in-time 31 December snapshot
evidence: Secondary sources (Vision IAS dated 2026-05-08, Drishti) report PSI 2024 release with 1,333 jails, sanctioned capacity 4.53 lakh, actual population 5.11 lakh, occupancy 112.7% (down from 120.8% in 2023), 95.8% male / 4.14% female / 122 transgender, 73% undertrial, Delhi highest occupancy at 194.6%. Dataful hosts four PSI collections (ids 1411, 1415, 1417 and dataset 19004) derived from these reports. The landing URL itself is an inferred path and was not opened.
how_to_obtain: Download from the Prison Statistics section of ncrb.gov.in; cleaner tabular versions at dataful.in collections 1411/1415/1417.
notes: Low priority for a crime map. Its one genuine use is as a denominator check on charge-sheeting and as a justice-system-outcome layer.

name: Finger Print in India (annual report)
publisher: National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Central Finger Print Bureau
caveats: Operational throughput statistics (slips searched, identifications made), not crime counts
No spatial value below state
evidence: NCRB absorbed CBI's Central Finger Print Bureau at its 1986 founding (Wikipedia), and the Bureau is the standard publisher of an annual fingerprint report. No URL surfaced in this session and ncrb.gov.in could not be browsed.
how_to_obtain: Check the Publications menu on ncrb.gov.in. If absent, RTI to CPIO, NCRB, NH-8 Mahipalpur, New Delhi 110037.
notes: Listed for completeness of the NCRB publication set. Irrelevant to mapping.

name: Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS)
caveats: This is the single richest crime dataset in India - FIR-level, police-station-keyed, near real time - and none of it is published in aggregate
No national public aggregate, no national FIR search for citizens; the 11 searches and 44 reports are for police/CBI/IB/ED/NIA only
Citizen-facing FIR view exists only through STATE portals, with wildly varying completeness, and several states expose only a subset of FIR types
Data quality varies by state; entry lags and back-dated entry are common
evidence: Wikipedia CCTNS article: cabinet approval 2009 with Rs 2,000 crore, pilot 4 Jan 2013, interconnects ~15,000 police stations and ~5,000 supervisory offices across 28 states and 8 UTs, Wipro built the Core Application Software, and a central citizen portal links to state citizen portals. PIB release 171422 covers the CCTNS Digital Police Portal launch. digitalpolice.gov.in/writereaddata/brief180917.pdf is an indexed MHA brief on CCTNS.
how_to_obtain: Aggregate CCTNS data is not published. Routes: (a) scrape each state's own CCTNS citizen portal for FIR listings - this is where police-station-level data actually exists and is the correct Phase 2 target; (b) RTI to each State Crime Records Bureau for monthly police-station-wise FIR counts by crime head - counts, not records, so it survives the s.8(1)(h) investigation exemption; (c) MHA/NCRB MoU for research access, no documented process.
notes: CCTNS is the reason a police.uk-style map is technically possible in India. The obstacle is policy, not engineering. Per-state portal scraping is a separate agent's scope but flag it here: the state citizen portals are downstream of CCTNS and carry the same schema.

name: Digital Police Portal (digitalpolice.gov.in)
caveats: NOT a national FIR search. It is an aggregator that hands off to state portals; the national criminal database behind it is restricted to law enforcement
Citizen services (online FIR/complaint registration, passport verification, case status, victim compensation) are routed to the relevant state system and availability differs by state
The citizen services endpoint is a login page; anonymous bulk access is not offered
evidence: PIB release 171422 'CCTNS Digital Police Portal launched to fast-track Criminal Justice System in the Country' and MHA's digitalpolice.gov.in/DigitalPolice/AboutUs were returned as indexed pages; secondary sources date the launch to 21 Aug 2017 and describe 11 searches and 44 reports available to police agencies only. The citizen endpoint https://www.digitalpolicecitizenservices.gov.in/centercitizen/login.htm is indexed as ':::CCTNS:::' login. None of these could be opened from this environment.
how_to_obtain: Browse from an unblocked network. For data, treat the state portals it links to as the real targets and catalogue them per state.
notes: Answering the brief's question directly: NO, nationwide citizen FIR SEARCH is not available. Nationwide citizen FIR FILING is claimed but is really a routing layer over state systems.

name: Inter-operable Criminal Justice System (ICJS / ICJS 2.0)
publisher: NCRB (nodal agency) with NIC; Ministry of Home Affairs
caveats: Integrates five pillars - Police (CCTNS), Courts (eCourts), Prisons (ePrisons), Forensics (eForensics), Prosecution (eProsecution) - but exposes nothing publicly
Data flow governed by a 'Data Sharing Matrix' approved by the Supreme Court e-Committee; that matrix does not include the public
The eCourts pillar IS publicly queryable, so ICJS's court-side data is reachable by another route
evidence: MHA pages mha.gov.in/en/commoncontent/inter-operable-criminal-justice-system-icjs and .../icjsncrb-administration were returned as indexed results; a PIB factsheet PDF (doc202262367401.pdf, June 2022) and an IIPA evaluation report (iipa.org.in/upload/project_report/pr36_1.pdf) describe the five pillars, NCRB as nodal agency with NIC as technology partner, MeghRaj cloud hosting, and ICJS 2.0's enterprise data lake.
how_to_obtain: No public data route. The stated intent that ICJS will enable 'national level crime analytics to be published at an increased frequency' is the hook for an RTI or a policy ask: request the analytics products already generated under ICJS 2.0.
notes: Worth watching. If NCRB ever publishes sub-annual crime analytics, ICJS 2.0's data lake is where it will come from.

name: Crime Multi Agency Centre (Cri-MAC)
caveats: Police-to-police alerting channel for heinous and inter-state crime; nothing public
No published aggregate of alert volumes
evidence: MHA Women Safety Division CCTNS page (indexed) states Cri-MAC was implemented on 12 March 2020 to let police stations and higher offices in all States/UTs share information on heinous crime and inter-state crime coordination.
how_to_obtain: Not obtainable. An RTI for annual counts of Cri-MAC alerts by state is plausible and would at best give a coarse heinous-crime-activity proxy.
notes: Catalogued for completeness. No map value.

name: National Database on Sexual Offenders (NDSO)
caveats: Explicitly law-enforcement-only. India deliberately did NOT build a US-style public sex offender registry
Contains convicted AND arrested/charged persons, so publication would be legally and ethically indefensible
Only the aggregate size is ever quoted (4.5 lakh+ entries at launch)
evidence: Launched 20 Sept 2018 alongside the Cyber Crime Prevention against Women and Children portal; maintained by NCRB and available only to law enforcement agencies (multiple secondary sources including a Business Standard report on 4.5 lakh entries).
how_to_obtain: Not obtainable and should not be pursued. An RTI for state-wise entry counts would yield only an arrest-volume proxy.
notes: DO NOT build any product feature on this. Publishing offender locations is out of scope for a lawful Indian crime map.

name: Talash (missing persons / unidentified dead body matching)
caveats: Internal matching service, not a public search
Overlaps functionally with ZIPNET and with state missing-persons portals
evidence: Described on the MHA CCTNS page as an NCRB-maintained IT-based public service for 'matching of missing persons and dead bodies', listed beside Vahan Samanvay. No standalone URL surfaced.
how_to_obtain: Ask NCRB whether Talash has a citizen front-end; if not, use the state missing-persons portals and ZIPNET instead.
notes: Missing-persons counts are a weak safety signal and a strong defamation risk. Low priority.

name: Vahan Samanvay (stolen / recovered vehicle matching)
caveats: Lookup-by-registration-number only; no bulk or area query, so it cannot produce vehicle-theft density
Historically had a public single-vehicle search; current status unverified
evidence: Named on the MHA CCTNS page as an NCRB IT-based public service for 'online matching for Stolen/Recovered vehicles'. No working URL surfaced in this session.
how_to_obtain: For theft density use the Crime in India property-crime tables and state CCTNS portals instead. Vahan Samanvay is a per-vehicle lookup and is not harvestable at volume without abusing it.
notes: Explicitly do not scrape. Per-record lookup services are the sort of thing a rate-limit and a legal notice are built for.

name: National Automated Fingerprint Identification System (NAFIS)
time_latest: live (1.06 crore records as of 31 Oct 2024)
caveats: Biometric database of arrested persons; no public access and none should be sought
Record counts are occasionally quoted in Parliament answers - that is the only public signal
evidence: Wikipedia 'National Crime Records Bureau' (fetched 2026-09-19) states NAFIS launched 17 Aug 2022, assigns a 10-digit National Fingerprint Number to every arrested person, holds 1.06 crore criminal fingerprint records as of 31 Oct 2024, and is connected to state fingerprint systems across all states and UTs.
how_to_obtain: n/a - not a public dataset.
notes: The only fact worth carrying forward is the NFN: it is the person-level join key across CCTNS/ICJS, which is why unit-level NCRB release will never happen without de-identification.

name: ZIPNET - Zonal Integrated Police Network
geo_coverage: Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Punjab, Chandigarh, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh
time_latest: live (7,880+ Delhi missing untraced 1 Jan - 23 Jul 2025; 1,486 unidentified bodies in the same window)
caveats: zipnet.in as given in the brief appears superseded: the live service is at zipnet.delhipolice.gov.in and Delhi Police recently relaunched an upgraded site
Not an NCRB system - it is a Delhi-Police-run consortium covering only 8 northern jurisdictions
Record-level personal data (names, photographs of missing persons and unidentified bodies). Republishing it on a map is a privacy and dignity minefield
Missing-person and unidentified-body counts do not measure crime
evidence: Search engine returned live section URLs at zipnet.delhipolice.gov.in for Missing Persons, Un-Identified Dead Bodies, Un-Identified Persons Found, Missing Mobiles and a vehicles/mobiles section, plus the site root. A July 2025 Tribune report gives the Delhi counts above and confirms member forces: Delhi, Haryana, UP, Rajasthan, Punjab, Chandigarh, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, with ZIPNET created in 2004.
how_to_obtain: Public HTML; paginated listing pages are scrapable. Check robots.txt first and rate-limit hard.
notes: Best use is COUNTS BY POLICE DISTRICT as a derived aggregate. Never republish the individual records.

name: Khoya-Paya / TrackChild, migrated to Mission Vatsalya Portal
publisher: Ministry of Women & Child Development (with NCRB/MHA linkage), NOT NCRB-owned
caveats: trackthemissingchild.gov.in services have been MIGRATED to missionvatsalya.wcd.gov.in - the old portal is no longer the active platform
Citizen-reported sightings are unverified by police, so counts mix police records with crowd reports
Children's identifying data; do not republish records
evidence: Indian government services catalogue lists the Khoya-Paya portal; the search synthesis states TrackChild services have migrated to the unified Mission Vatsalya Portal at missionvatsalya.wcd.gov.in and that Khoya-Paya's missing/sighted-children application has been integrated into it. PIB release 175406 covers online tracking portals for missing children.
how_to_obtain: Public web; check whether Mission Vatsalya exposes state/district counts before scraping records.
notes: Outside NCRB's ownership but inside the brief. Its only map-relevant output is district counts of reported missing children, which NCRB's Crime Against Children chapter already covers more consistently.

name: NCRB unit-level / FIR-level microdata release
caveats: NCRB DOES NOT RELEASE UNIT-LEVEL DATA. There is no documented microdata access programme, no data enclave, no researcher application form - unlike MoSPI/NSSO which does run one
The FIR is the basic unit of the annual reports, but only aggregates are ever published
NCRB additionally withheld district-wise data entirely for reference years 2016 and 2017, with no stated reason, and released no machine-readable files for those years
evidence: ThePrint's analysis of NCRB crime data states plainly that NCRB does not release unit-level data and that for 2016 and 2017 it did not release district-wise data or machine-readable formats. No NCRB microdata policy page, application form or data-enclave documentation surfaced in any search.
how_to_obtain: Three realistic routes, in ascending cost: (1) RTI to CPIO, NCRB, MHA, NH-8 Mahipalpur, New Delhi 110037, asking for district-wise and police-station-wise COUNTS by crime head - counts are not exempt under s.8(1)(h); (2) State Crime Records Bureau RTIs, which are far more likely to yield police-station-level tables; (3) an academic MoU with NCRB via a recognised institution - no published process, must be negotiated.
notes: This is the defining constraint of the whole project. Everything finer than district in India comes from state police, not from NCRB. Formats not recorded by the researching agent; confirm during the URL verification pass.

name: RTI route to NCRB tabulations not published in Crime in India
publisher: NCRB CPIO / State Crime Records Bureaux
caveats: NCRB routinely transfers requests to states under s.6(3) because it holds what states send it, not the underlying records
s.8(1)(h) (impeding investigation) is the standard refusal for anything record-level; ask for counts, never records
Responses arrive as scanned PDFs of printed tables
evidence: No NCRB RTI page could be opened. RTI activity around NCRB publication delays is referenced in CJP's coverage, and stat@ncrb.gov.in surfaced in a search synthesis as NCRB's statistics contact address (unconfirmed).
how_to_obtain: File at rtionline.gov.in against Ministry of Home Affairs / NCRB. Draft the request as: 'Crime-head-wise number of cases registered, for each police district and each police station in <state>, for calendar years 2022-2025, in machine-readable format.' Expect a s.6(3) transfer to the state; file the state RTI in parallel.
notes: Budget for a 36-state RTI campaign if police-station granularity is a product requirement. This is the single biggest cost line in Phase 2.

name: NCRB datasets on data.gov.in (OGD Platform India)
publisher: NIC / Open Government Data Platform India, publishing NCRB data
time_latest: unknown - the district catalogs are believed stale, ending around 2012-2014
caveats: THE CLEANEST MACHINE-READABLE DISTRICT SERIES NCRB HAS EVER SHIPPED, and it appears frozen. Verify the latest year before relying on it
District names are raw strings with no stable code; they do not join to LGD or Census codes without a crosswalk
Only covers a subset of crime heads (murder, rape, kidnapping & abduction, dacoity, robbery, theft, riots, crimes against women)
evidence: Two district-level OGD catalog URLs were returned as indexed results with matching titles: 'District-wise crimes under various sections of Indian Penal Code (IPC) crimes' and 'District-wise crimes committed against Women'. The search synthesis lists the covered heads as murder, rape, kidnapping and abduction, dacoity, robbery, theft, riots and crimes against women (rape, K&A, dowry death, assault on women with intent to outrage modesty, insult to modesty, cruelty by husband or relatives, importation of girls). data.gov.in is egress-blocked here so the year range and row counts are unconfirmed.
how_to_obtain: Free registration at data.gov.in gives an API key; resources are downloadable as CSV/XLSX/JSON and queryable through the OGD resource API.
notes: Another agent covers portals. Flagging it here because THIS is where NCRB's district series exists in usable form - far better than OCRing PDFs. Confirming its terminal year is a Phase 2 day-one task.

name: NCRB series on NDAP (National Data & Analytics Platform, NITI Aayog)
caveats: NDAP's selling point is a standardised district key across datasets - that is exactly the crosswalk this project needs
Coverage of NCRB series on NDAP is unverified; may be headline tables only
evidence: No NDAP URL for an NCRB dataset surfaced in this session and ndap.niti.gov.in is egress-blocked (curl CONNECT 403). Listed on the strength of NDAP's documented mandate to host and harmonise central-ministry datasets.
how_to_obtain: Register at ndap.niti.gov.in, search 'NCRB' / 'Crime in India', and specifically check whether NDAP has applied its district harmonisation to the NCRB tables.
notes: If NDAP has already solved district-name harmonisation for NCRB, it eliminates the largest single piece of ingestion work. Verify early.

name: NCRB collections on Dataful (Factly Data Labs)
caveats: Commercial. Free preview, paid download for most datasets; redistribution inside a public map is a licensing question, not a technical one
Observed collections are YEAR-AND-STATE-WISE, not district-wise - Dataful appears to have digitised the state tables, not the district ones
Derived, not authoritative; every figure must be reconciled to the NCRB PDF before publication
evidence: Indexed Dataful items include collection 1108 'NCRB Crime in India (Summary)', dataset 21867 'Year and State wise Number of IPC/BNS Crimes', 21547 'NCRB - Crimes against Women: Year and State wise', 22522 'Year, State and City wise Number of IPC Crimes', plus prison collections 1411/1415/1417 and dataset 19004. dataful.in is egress-blocked here so row counts and prices are unconfirmed.
how_to_obtain: Browse dataful.in, check per-dataset licence, contact Factly for a bulk/nonprofit arrangement before designing a pipeline around it.
notes: Best fallback if OCRing NCRB PDFs proves too slow for the STATE series. Does not solve the district problem.

name: NCRB reports mirrored on OpenCity (data.opencity.in CKAN)
caveats: A mirror of NCRB PDFs, mostly not re-tabulated
CKAN API available, which makes enumerating what they hold cheap
evidence: Indexed CKAN dataset pages for Crime in India 2022, 2023 and 2024 and for ADSI 2024, plus a facet search showing '26 datasets found for ncrb.gov.in' filtered to PDF. The 2024 page is described as including IPC/BNS crime-head datasets for 2022-24. Domain is egress-blocked here.
how_to_obtain: CKAN API: https://data.opencity.in/api/3/action/package_search?q=ncrb - this is the cheapest way to get a complete manifest of mirrored NCRB files with checksums and sizes.
notes: VALUABLE WORKAROUND. If ncrb.gov.in is slow, rate-limited or geo-fenced for your ingestion host, pull the same PDFs from this CKAN with proper metadata.

name: Statistical Year Book India - Chapter 37, Crime Statistics
publisher: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), sourcing NCRB
lag: follows NCRB, plus MoSPI's own lag
caveats: Pure re-publication of NCRB headline tables; adds nothing below state level
Useful only as an independent transcription to cross-check OCR of NCRB PDFs
evidence: Indexed as 'CHAPTER 37 CRIME STATISTICS' at mospi.gov.in. Domain egress-blocked here.
how_to_obtain: Direct PDF download.
notes: Include as a validation source, not a data source.

name: NCRB tabulations released through Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha answers
publisher: Ministry of Home Affairs, answering Parliament; data compiled by NCRB
lag: often FRESHER than the published report - MPs get years NCRB has not yet released
caveats: Annexures are scanned or text PDFs of printed tables; formats are inconsistent question to question
Coverage is whatever an MP happened to ask; no systematic series
Occasionally contains cuts NCRB never publishes (district-wise, scheme-wise, portal-wise counts)
evidence: Two indexed parliamentary annexure PDFs surfaced: sansad.in/getFile/annex/266/AU1119_bGpZrf.pdf, whose snippet opens '(a): The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) compiles...', and an MHA Lok Sabha answer PDF dated 24 March 2026 (LS24032026/5252.pdf) concerning missing-children portals. how_to_obtain: Search sansad.in question archives for 'NCRB', 'CCTNS', 'crime against women' by session. MHA mirrors its own answers under mha.gov.in/MHA1/Par2017/pdfs/par<year>-pdfs/.
notes: UNDERRATED SOURCE. This is the most reliable way to get post-2024 crime figures before Crime in India 2025 appears, and the only routine way NCRB publishes cuts it otherwise withholds.
